1.title: A time of waiting. A movement within. A life drawing near.

p.1: Pregnancy is a time apart, lived differently by each person.
p.2: For the mother, it is also lived in the body: the body changes, its rhythm shifts and something gradually takes shape.
p.3: When a father, a second parent or a partner is present, their experience is necessarily different. Some feel like parents straight away. Others need time.
p.4: And sometimes pregnancy is lived alone, by choice or because life decided otherwise.
p.5: The bond with the child can grow through scans, conversations, movements felt, thoughts addressed to them, or simply through the images that slowly take shape.
p.6: This time can bring all kinds of feelings: joy, impatience, pride, worry, a sense of responsibility, fear of not being up to it, or questions about the place the child will take in your life.
p.7: Pregnancy is not always calm or light. It can hold joy, but also discomfort, doubts, fragile moments or a sense of loneliness. Life goes on around it: personal, family, relationship or work events can also cross this time.
p.8: During these months, a bond begins to form. The child is thought about, imagined, sometimes named, sometimes simply felt.
p.9: This bond does not need to be constant or intense to be real. It can be quiet, changing, silent. It grows in its own way.
p.10: Here, telling the story of the pregnancy is not about getting it right. It is about recognising this time as a human journey, made of strengths and fragilities.
p.11: This Carnet is here to hold this experience as it was, without correcting it, without idealising it.

1.quote: Every pregnancy has its own story, its own rhythm and its own way of creating a bond.

2.intro:

2.quote: The bond does not need to be immediate to start growing.

4.title: Hands on the belly

p.1: From time to time, take a few moments around the belly.
p.2: The mother-to-be can simply place her hands on her belly and speak to the child.
p.3: If other people share this wait — a father, a second parent, a brother, a sister or someone close — they can join in too, if it feels natural.
p.4: Call the child by their name if it has already been chosen, by a nickname, or simply talk to them.
p.5: There is nothing in particular to get right. A few seconds can be enough.
p.6:
A hand resting.

A word.

A silence.

A movement felt.

4.quote: In this simple gesture, the bond is already there.
4.invite: We invite anyone who wishes to keep a trace of this moment to photograph it, film it or simply record a few words, and place it in Carnet de Vie. One day the child will be able to discover something of this bond that was already forming before they were born.

p.1: During pregnancy, the bond with the child can begin to form long before birth. This bond can be very present, but also quieter, changing or hard to feel.
p.2: Daniel Stern (1934–2012) – American psychiatrist and psychoanalyst, specialist in early development and parent–child relationships.
p.3: Stern’s work explored in particular the images that form around the child and around parenthood.
p.4: During pregnancy, a person can gradually imagine the child, anticipate certain interactions and begin to picture themselves in their new role.
p.5: But there is no single way to experience this bond.
p.6: Some people feel very close to the child even before birth. For others, the bond becomes more real with the scans, the baby’s movements, the birth or the first interactions.
p.7: So birth is not the end point of a bond that should already be fully in place. It opens a new stage in a relationship that will keep on growing.

points.1: The bond with the child can begin before birth.
points.2: It can be intense, quiet, changing, or form later on.
points.3: There is no single way of already feeling like a parent during pregnancy.
points.4: The images imagined during pregnancy will change on meeting the real child.
points.5: The bond will keep growing long after birth.

p.1: Pregnancy and the time around birth can bring a particular sensitivity to the child and to everything about their arrival.
p.2: Donald Winnicott (1896–1971) – British paediatrician and psychoanalyst, specialist in early emotional development and the mother–baby relationship.
p.3: Winnicott put forward the idea of “primary maternal preoccupation” to describe a state of heightened sensitivity that appears in many mothers towards the end of pregnancy and in the first weeks after birth.
p.4: This particular availability can help the mother become very attentive to the newborn’s signals and needs.
p.5: It does not mean a mother should constantly feel an intense closeness to her baby, nor that all women experience pregnancy or the first weeks in the same way.
p.6: The concept describes a possible process, not a model one should match.

points.1: A particular sensitivity to the baby can appear during pregnancy and around birth.
points.2: This availability can help with gradually adjusting to the newborn’s needs.
points.3: Not all mothers experience this time in the same way.
points.4: Not feeling an intense closeness straight away does not mean the bond cannot grow.
points.5: The relationship with the child develops gradually through real interactions.

entourage.title: A child’s arrival and the bonds around you

p.1: The arrival of a child changes the balance of relationships around the person becoming a parent.
p.2: When there is a couple, responsibilities, expectations and each person’s place can shift. The arrival of a child can deeply change the couple’s life: the daily rhythm changes, responsibilities grow and new adjustments become necessary.
p.3: John Gottman (born 1942) – American psychologist, a researcher known for his work on couple and family relationships.
p.4: His research on couples has looked in particular at the transition to parenthood and the changes in relationships that can come with a child’s arrival.
p.5: Tiredness, how responsibilities are shared, less time for the couple and each person’s different expectations can alter the earlier balance.
p.6: When there is a couple, being able to talk about these changes, express one’s needs and recognise that each person may experience this transition differently helps gradually build a new balance.
p.7: But support around a child’s arrival does not necessarily rest on a couple.
p.8: For someone going through pregnancy alone, by choice or because life’s circumstances led them there, ties with family, friends or other close people can take on a particularly important place.
p.9: So there is no single relationship setting for welcoming a child. What also matters is being able to find, where possible, bonds to lean on.

points.1: A child’s arrival can change your relationships with the people around you.
points.2: When there is a couple, each person may experience this transition differently.
points.3: Tiredness and new responsibilities can change the balance of a relationship.
points.4: Support can come from a partner, but also from family, friends or other close people.
points.5: There is no single family or relationship setting for welcoming a child.

closing.1: I couldn’t see you yet. And yet, every day, you were already changing my life.
